item.title: Indian Affairs: Legal Framework for Probate and Other Factors Limit Interior’s Options to Improve Its Process
item.description:
What GAO Found
GAO’s analysis of the Department of the Interior’s probate data shows that its ongoing probate caseload grew from about 19,000 cases in October 2013, to about 55,000 cases in April 2026. This was due, in part, to an increase in case files in the case preparation phase, the first stage in the probate process after reporting a death, and a decrease in the number of probate hearings held. GAO found that 80 percent of nationwide probate cases were in the preparation phase.
Interior has a statutory responsibility to probate all trust and restricted fee estates and legal requirements to provide notice of those cases to interested parties. According to Interior, fractionation—which occurs when an individual parcel of trust and restricted fee land has many owners with undivided, small interests in the parcel—has increased the number of future estates to probate. Solutions to address fractionation must be within constitutional limitations. This legal framework, both statutory and constitutional, limits Interior’s options to improve the probate case process.
BIA has taken some steps to improve the probate process, such as easing access to vital records between Interior and state governments. However, the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA), and Bureau of Trust Funds Administration (BTFA) have not analyzed the number of staff and skills needed to efficiently carry out probate. GAO found that these three agencies experienced staff losses and staffing vacancies. BIA, OHA, and BTFA have acknowledged the importance of such analysis but have not yet developed workforce plans. Developing such plans would help Interior prevent delays in probate, which can result in hardships for potential heirs that are inconsistent with its mission.

In addition, BIA, BTFA, OHA, and the Office of the Solicitor told GAO that some probate process reforms may be possible, but they have not yet explored such options to determine if they are viable or what regulatory changes or statutory authorizations would be needed. By jointly coordinating to identify reform proposals and submit them to Congress or initiate any rulemaking for the regulatory reforms, actionable steps can be taken towards a timelier and more efficient distribution of trust and restricted fee assets.
Why GAO Did This Study
Interior is responsible for probating the trust and restricted fee assets of thousands of Indians who die each year. Probate is the legal process by which assets are distributed to heirs using the applicable tribal, federal, or state law governing distribution of a decedent’s estate, among other things. Interior has several offices that are responsible for carrying out the probate process, from gathering family information to adjudicating decisions and distributing assets to heirs. However, Tribes and tribal organizations have raised questions about the length of time taken to probate these estates.
GAO was asked to review Interior’s probate process. This report examines (1) Interior’s ongoing probate caseload from October 2013 through April 2026; (2) factors that affect Interior’s ability to probate trust and restricted fee assets; and (3) actions Interior has taken to improve the probate process and what further actions are needed.
GAO reviewed laws, regulations, policies, and guidance related to Interior’s probate process; analyzed BIA data on probate cases from October 2013 through April 2026 (the most recent and complete data); and interviewed agency officials and a nongeneralizable sample of Tribes and tribal-serving organizations.
